mainTopic: Limits of acquiring through ארבע אמות, and whether a קטנה acquires through חצר: is a חצר like a hand or like an agent?
overview: This amud finishes the discussion of ריש לקיש's rule that a person's ארבע אמות acquire an item for him. רב פפא says the rule does not work in a בעל הבית's field, even where a poor person may collect פאה. רבי יעקב בר אידי challenges the rule from our משנה about someone who falls on a found item. The גמרא answers that by falling, the man showed he did not want to acquire through his four cubits. רב ששת answers differently: the rule works only in a quiet סמטא or at the sides of a רשות הרבים, not where crowds push. Then a new מחלוקת begins: can a קטנה acquire through her חצר and ארבע אמות? The גמרא explains that it depends on whether a חצר works like a hand (יד) or like an agent (שליחות). It defends the agency view against the rule of אין שליח לדבר עבירה with two answers, from רבינא and רב סמא, and shows where those answers differ. Finally, it limits the dispute to מציאה, since for a גט everyone agrees a חצר counts as her hand.

steps.title: רב פפא: The four cubits rule does not apply in a homeowner's field
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers the challenge from the פאה case. The חכמים made the four-cubits rule only for public places, not for a field that belongs to a בעל הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: When the Sages made the rule that four cubits acquire for a person, that was in the world at large. In a homeowner's field, the Sages did not make this rule for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a new answer to the earlier question about the poor person collecting פאה. The four-cubits rule simply does not apply inside a בעל הבית's field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier challenge was this: why doesn't the poor person's four cubits acquire the פאה for him? רב פפא says the תקנה only covers ownerless public spaces. Since the פאה case happens in a private field, it was never included, so ריש לקיש's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages instituted (made a rabbinic enactment)
Four cubits, the space around a person that can acquire for him
In the world at large, meaning public places
Homeowner, the owner of the field

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב פפא is rejecting ריש לקיש's rule. He keeps it and only marks where it applies.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי תַּקִּינוּ לֵיה רַבָּנַן אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת –
phrases.english: When the Sages instituted four cubits for him (to acquire),
that was in the world at large;
in a field belonging to a homeowner
the Sages did not institute it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כִּי תַּקִּינוּ לֵיה רַבָּנַן אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another answer to the earlier challenge from the פאה case against ריש לקיש.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule (location-based)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The four-cubits rule works everywhere, so it should work for the poor person in the field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule was only made for public spaces, not for a בעל הבית's field.

steps.title: The Torah let the poor person walk in the field, but did not make it his courtyard
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא heads off an objection. The Torah gave the poor person rights in the field, but only the right to walk there and collect פאה. It did not make the field count as his חצר for acquiring.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even though the Torah gave him rights in the field: when the Torah gave him rights, it was to walk in it and collect פאה. For it to count as his courtyard, the Torah did not give him that.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers a question before anyone asks it. One might think the poor person has rights in the field, so his four cubits should work there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the Torah gave the poor person a kind of ownership in the field. רב פפא says that right is narrow: walking and gathering. It does not make the land like his own חצר, which is what the four-cubits rule is based on.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah (literally 'the Merciful One') granted him rights
To walk
The corner of the field left for the poor
His courtyard, property that acquires for its owner

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, the four cubits work only where the person is not on someone else's private land. Having a right to walk and collect there is not the same as owning it.

phrases.english: And even though
the Torah granted him rights in it,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the בעל הבית's field, where the poor person collects פאה.

phrases.english: when the Torah granted him rights,
it was to walk in it and to collect pe'ah;
for it to be considered his courtyard
the Torah did not grant him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּזְכָה לֵיהּ רַחֲמָנָא בְּגַוַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends step 1 against an unspoken objection about the poor person's rights in the field.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the limited scope of a Torah-given right
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The poor person's Torah-given rights in the field make it like his own land.
steps.terutzMaskana: His rights cover only walking and gathering, not ownership like a חצר.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה of the person who fell on a found item
steps.stepSummary: רבא reports that רבי יעקב בר אידי challenged ריש לקיש from our משנה. If someone falls on a found item and another person picks it up, the one who picked it up gets it. But the first person's four cubits should already have acquired it for him!
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: רבי יעקב בר אידי raises an objection from נזיקין: If someone saw a found item and fell on it, and another came and took hold of it, the one who took hold of it acquired it. And if you say a person's four cubits acquire for him everywhere, let his own four cubits acquire it for him!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge is brought against ריש לקיש's four-cubits rule. The source is our own משנה about falling on a found item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first person was clearly within four cubits of the item. He was lying right on it! If four cubits acquire everywhere, he should own it before the second person grabs it. Yet the משנה gives it to the grabber.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection
The tractate of damages (here, our own tractate)
A found item
Took hold of it / seized it

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: מוֹתֵיב רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידִי נְזִיקִין:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi raises an objection from Nezikin:
phrases.notes: בבא קמא, בבא מציעא and בבא בתרא were once one big tractate called נזיקין, so the source is our own משנה.

phrases.english: If he saw a found item
and fell upon it,
and another came and seized it,
the one who seized it acquired it.
And if you say

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל אָדָם קוֹנוֹת לוֹ בְּכׇל מָקוֹם –
phrases.english: that a person's four cubits acquire for him everywhere,
let his own four cubits acquire it for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, מוֹתֵיב רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידִי נְזִיקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the פאה challenge to a new challenge from our משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's rule that a person's four cubits acquire for him everywhere
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The man who fell on the item was within his four cubits, so he should have acquired it. Yet the משנה awards it to the one who seized it.

steps.title: Answer: He never said 'I will acquire'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a case where the person who fell never said 'אקני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where he did not say: 'I will acquire.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case in the משנה. The first person never stated that he wanted to acquire the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the four cubits need the person to declare his intent to acquire. Since he stayed silent, his four cubits did not take effect. That is why the second person wins.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to limit a source to a specific situation)
'I will acquire', a spoken statement of intent to acquire

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
A case where he did not say: 'I will acquire.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The man in the משנה should have acquired through his four cubits.
steps.terutzMaskana: He didn't say 'אקני', so his four cubits did not acquire.

steps.title: But why should saying it matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. If the חכמים made a rule that four cubits acquire, why would it matter whether he said 'אקני'?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the Sages instituted it, then when he did not say it, so what?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 4. A rabbinic rule should work on its own, without any spoken statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the חכמים gave the four cubits the power to acquire, it seems they should work automatically, like a person's חצר. So the missing words 'אקני' should not stop the acquisition.

keyTerms.meaning: What of it? So what difference does it make?

phrases.english: But if the Sages instituted it,
then when he did not say it, what of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי תַּקּוּן רַבָּנַן, כִּי לָא אֲמַר מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that he didn't say 'אקני'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rabbinic enactment should work automatically, so a spoken declaration should not be needed.

steps.title: By falling on it, he showed he wanted to acquire only by falling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that falling on the item showed his intent. He wanted to acquire by falling on it, not through his four cubits, so the four cubits did not acquire for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he fell on it, he revealed his mind: he is happy to acquire by falling, but he is not happy to acquire through four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of step 5. The problem is not that he stayed silent. The problem is that his action showed he chose a different way of acquiring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Falling on the item showed he was relying only on falling, and falling is not a valid קנין. That means he gave up on the four-cubits method. Since he didn't want it, it didn't work for him, and the second person acquired.

keyTerms.meaning: He revealed his intent
Falling (on the item)
It is pleasing / acceptable to him

steps.whatToRemember: The four cubits can be blocked by the person's own behavior. If his actions show he is choosing a different method, the four cubits do not acquire for him.

phrases.english: Since he fell upon it,
he revealed his intention
that it is acceptable to him to acquire by falling,

phrases.aramaic: בְּאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת לָא נִיחָא לֵיהּ דְּנִקְנֵי.
phrases.english: and through four cubits it is not acceptable to him to acquire.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּנָפַל עָלֶיהָ, גַּלִּי דַּעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5 and explains the answer of step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rabbinic four cubits work automatically, whether or not he speaks.
steps.terutzMaskana: His falling showed he did not want the four-cubits method, so it did not acquire for him.

steps.title: רב ששת: The rule applies only in a quiet alleyway, not in a crowded public street
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת gives a different answer to the challenge from our משנה. The חכמים made the four-cubits rule only for a סמטא where crowds don't push, not for a crowded רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: When the Sages instituted it, it was in an alleyway where the crowds do not push. In the public domain, where the crowds push, the Sages did not institute it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת offers another way to answer רבי יעקב בר אידי's challenge. The four cubits only acquire in a quiet place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a crowded street, other people are always filling the space around you, so it can't count as 'your' four cubits. In a quiet סמטא, the space can be considered yours. So the משנה is talking about a busy רשות הרבים, where the four cubits never applied.

keyTerms.meaning: An alleyway / side street with little traffic
The crowds push / press
The public domain, a busy public area

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical limit on the four-cubits rule: it only works where the space around a person is not crowded by others.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
When the Sages instituted it,
it was in an alleyway, where the crowds do not push.
In the public domain, where the crowds push,
the Sages did not institute it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר: כִּי תַּקִּינוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the challenge of step 3, instead of the answer about 'אקני'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule (location-based)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The four cubits acquire everywhere, even in a busy street.
steps.terutzMaskana: The four cubits acquire only in a quiet סמטא, not in a crowded רשות הרבים.

steps.title: But he said the rule works everywhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ששת: ריש לקיש said four cubits acquire 'everywhere,' so how can the rule be limited to a סמטא?
steps.simpleTranslation: But he said 'in every place'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב ששת's answer from step 7. ריש לקיש's own words say the four cubits acquire 'in every place.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת said the rule only works in a quiet סמטא, not in a crowded רשות הרבים. But 'every place' sounds like it should include the רשות הרבים too. So the wording of ריש לקיש's rule seems to contradict רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: In every place, the wording of ריש לקיש's rule about four cubits
He says

phrases.english: But he says 'in every place'!
phrases.notes: 'He' is ריש לקיש, who said a person's four cubits acquire for him in every place.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא בְּכׇל מָקוֹם קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's limitation from step 7 using the wording of ריש לקיש's rule
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that the four-cubits rule applies only in a סמטא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ריש לקיש said 'in every place,' which seems to include the רשות הרבים

steps.title: 'Everywhere' only adds the sides of the public area
steps.stepSummary: The word 'everywhere' does not include the crowded רשות הרבים itself. It comes to include the sides of the רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Every place' comes to include the sides of the public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. 'Every place' does not mean literally everywhere. It means the rule also works at the edges of a רשות הרבים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sides of a public area are not crowded the way the middle is, so they are like a סמטא. The word 'everywhere' adds those spots, which you might have thought were left out. רב ששת's limit stays in place, and the crowded middle is still excluded.

keyTerms.meaning: To include, to bring in an extra case
The sides or edges of the public domain

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב ששת, the ד׳ אמות rule works only where crowds don't push: a סמטא, or the sides of a רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: 'Every place' —
is to include the sides of the public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל מָקוֹם לְאֵתוֹיֵי צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 by narrowing the meaning of 'every place'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word: 'every place' adds a borderline case and does not mean everywhere
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Every place' includes the crowded רשות הרבים
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Every place' includes only the sides of the רשות הרבים, which are not crowded

steps.title: Can a minor girl acquire through her courtyard and four cubits?
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש, quoting אבא כהן ברדלא, says a קטנה has no חצר and no ד׳ אמות for acquiring. רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי ינאי, says she has both.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said in the name of אבא כהן ברדלא: a minor girl has no courtyard and has no four cubits. רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי ינאי: she has a courtyard and she has four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a disagreement about whether a קטנה can acquire through her חצר or her ד׳ אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person's חצר and ד׳ אמות can acquire an item for them without picking it up. The question is whether these tools also work for a girl who is under age. One opinion says no to both, and the other says yes to both.

keyTerms.meaning: A minor girl, not yet of age
Courtyard; a person's property can acquire items placed in it for its owner
The four cubits around a person, which can acquire for them
The תנא whom ריש לקיש quotes

phrases.english: And ריש לקיש said
in the name of אבא כהן ברדלא:
A minor girl has no courtyard,
phrases.notes: He means her courtyard can't acquire things for her. She can still own a courtyard.

phrases.english: and she has no four cubits.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמַר:
phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי ינאי:
She has a courtyard,
and she has four cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם אַבָּא כֹּהֵן בַּרְדְּלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement of ריש לקיש, linked to the earlier topic of acquiring through ד׳ אמות
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אבא כהן ברדלא: a קטנה cannot acquire through her חצר or her ד׳ אמות. רבי ינאי: she can acquire through both.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what idea the two opinions disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind the מחלוקת. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to find the basic idea that leads one side to say 'yes' and the other to say 'no.'

keyTerms.meaning: About what do they disagree? The standard question asking for the root of a מחלוקת

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the מחלוקת in step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The idea at the root of the disagreement about a קטנה's חצר and ד׳ אמות

steps.title: Is a courtyard like a hand or like an agent?
steps.stepSummary: One view holds a חצר works like a person's hand, and a קטנה has a hand. The other holds a חצר works like שליחות (agency), and a קטנה has no agency.
steps.simpleTranslation: One master holds that a courtyard was included because of her hand. Just as she has a hand, she also has a courtyard. The other master holds that a courtyard was included because of agency. Just as she has no agency, she also has no courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the disagreement depends on why a חצר can acquire at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a חצר works like an extension of your hand, a קטנה can use it, because she can acquire with her own hand. If a חצר works like an agent acting for you, she cannot use it, because a קטנה has no power of שליחות. רבי ינאי holds the 'hand' view, and אבא כהן ברדלא holds the 'agency' view.

keyTerms.meaning: Hand; a person acquires something by taking it into their hand
Agency, acting through an agent
Was included, was added as a valid way to acquire
One master holds

steps.whatToRemember: The question of whether a קטנה acquires through her חצר depends on the reason a חצר works. If it works like a hand, she can acquire through it. If it works like an agent, she cannot.
steps.confusionAlert: The first 'מר' here is רבי ינאי, who says she can acquire, and the second 'מר' is אבא כהן ברדלא, who says she cannot. That is the opposite order from step 10.
steps.whyThisMatters: The question 'is a חצר like a hand or like an agent?' comes up as a basic idea in many סוגיות about acquiring.

phrases.english: One master holds
phrases.notes: This is רבי ינאי, the one who said she has a courtyard.

phrases.english: a courtyard was included because of her hand,
just as she has a hand —
she also has a courtyard.
And the other master holds
phrases.notes: This is אבא כהן ברדלא, the one ריש לקיש quoted.

phrases.english: a courtyard was included because of agency,
and just as she has no agency —
she also has no courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר חָצֵר מִשּׁוּם יָדָהּ אִיתְרַבַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether a חצר works like a hand (so a קטנה can use it) or like שליחות (so she cannot).

steps.title: Can anyone really say a courtyard works through agency?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether anyone could hold that חצר works through שליחות, and quotes a ברייתא about a thief's roof, yard, and enclosure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really anyone who says a courtyard acquires because of agency? But a ברייתא teaches: 'In his hand' only tells me about his hand. How do I know the law also applies to his roof, his yard, and his enclosure? The verse says 'shall surely be found,' which means in any place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view from Step 12 that a חצר works like שליחות. It brings a ברייתא as its source, and the next step explains why this ברייתא is a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא teaches that a גנב pays double when the stolen item is found in his roof, yard, or enclosure, not only in his hand. So a thief's courtyard takes hold of stolen property for him. The next step shows why that cannot fit the view that a חצר is a שליח.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא? (introduces a source used to challenge)
In his hand (his possession)
His roof
A fenced enclosure, usually behind a house
Shall surely be found (the doubled wording teaches 'in any place')

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is about a thief paying double, not about lost objects. The גמרא uses it because it shows a courtyard acquiring for its owner, even when the owner is doing something wrong.

phrases.english: Is there anyone who says
that a courtyard was included because of agency?
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
"In his hand": I only know about his hand.
phrases.notes: שמות 22:3. This is the פסוק about a thief caught with the stolen animal, who pays double.

phrases.english: His roof, his yard, and his enclosure, from where do we know?
The verse teaches: "shall surely be found,"
which means in any place.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אִיכָּא מַאן דְּאָמַר חָצֵר מִשּׁוּם שְׁלִיחוּת אִיתְרַבַּאי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the agency side of the dispute explained in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that חצר works through שליחות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא shows a thief's courtyard acquires stolen goods for him. The next step explains why that clashes with agency.

steps.title: A courtyard as agent would mean agency for a sin
steps.stepSummary: If a חצר were a שליח, the thief's courtyard would be a שליח for theft, but we hold אין שליח לדבר עבירה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think a courtyard was included because of agency, then we would have found agency for a sin. But we hold there is no agency for a sin!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out why the ברייתא is a problem. If a חצר is a שליח, then the thief's courtyard is acting as his agent to steal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule, אין שליח לדבר עבירה: you cannot make someone your agent to do a sin for you. Yet the ברייתא makes the thief liable through his courtyard. So a חצר must work like a hand, not like an agent.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it would enter your mind (if you were to think)
There is no agency for a sin; the sender is not responsible for the agent's sin
We hold, it is established for us

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the rule of אין שליח לדבר עבירה becomes a test for deciding how a חצר works.

phrases.english: And if it would enter your mind
that a courtyard was included because of agency,

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן מָצִינוּ שָׁלִיחַ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה,
phrases.english: if so, we have found agency for a sin,

phrases.aramaic: וְקַיְימָא לַן אֵין שָׁלִיחַ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה!
phrases.english: but we hold there is no agency for a sin!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ חָצֵר מִשּׁוּם שְׁלִיחוּת אִיתְרַבַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge by explaining the problem with the ברייתא from Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that חצר works through שליחות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a חצר is an agent, the ברייתא would allow agency for theft. That contradicts אין שליח לדבר עבירה.

steps.title: No agency for a sin only applies when the agent can be liable
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that אין שליח לדבר עבירה only applies when the agent himself is subject to liability. A courtyard is not, so its owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: When do we say there is no agency for a sin? When the agent is someone who can be held liable. But a courtyard cannot be held liable, so the one who sent it, its owner, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends the view that a חצר works through שליחות. He limits the rule of אין שליח לדבר עבירה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says the agent, not the sender, carries the sin. That only makes sense when the agent is someone who can be held responsible. A courtyard cannot be responsible, so the liability goes back to the owner, and the ברייתא fits the agency view.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer here
Someone subject to liability, who can be held responsible
The one who sent him (the sender)

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer narrows when אין שליח לדבר עבירה applies, and the next step will test that limit.

phrases.english: רבינא said:
Where do we say
that there is no agency for a sin?
Where the agent is subject to liability,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּחָצֵר דְּלָאו בַּר חִיּוּבָא הוּא –
phrases.english: but with a courtyard, which is not subject to liability,
its sender is liable.
phrases.notes: The "sender" of a courtyard is simply its owner, here the thief.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: הֵיכָא אָמְרִינַן דְּאֵין שָׁלִיחַ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 13-14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of a rule (אין שליח לדבר עבירה applies only to an agent who can be liable).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought אין שליח לדבר עבירה applies to every agent, so a courtyard agent could never make the thief liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule only applies when the agent can carry liability. A courtyard cannot, so the owner is liable.

steps.title: What about sending a woman or a slave to steal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבינא: by his logic, someone who sends a woman and a slave to steal should be liable, since they are not subject to liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, take someone who tells a woman and a slave, 'Go out and steal for me.' They are not subject to liability. Would you really say the sender is liable?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests רבינא's rule on a real case. It points to agents who cannot be held liable and asks whether the sender is then liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By רבינא's rule, whenever the agent cannot be liable, the sender becomes liable. A woman and a slave are agents who are not liable in the same way, yet it sounds wrong to make the sender pay. This is offered as a strong objection to רבינא.

keyTerms.meaning: But now, if so (introduces an extreme result of the previous answer)
A woman and a slave
Would it really be so? (a question of surprise)

phrases.english: But if so,
one who says to a woman and a slave:
"Go out and steal for me"
since they are not subject to liability,
phrases.notes: A married woman and a slave have no money of their own to pay with, so they can't be made to pay.

phrases.english: is the one who sent them really liable?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, הָאוֹמֵר לְאִשָּׁה וְעֶבֶד: ״צְאוּ גִּנְבוּ לִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer from Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's rule that the sender is liable whenever the agent is not subject to liability.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A woman and a slave are agents who are not subject to liability, so רבינא's rule would make the sender liable. That result seems unacceptable.

steps.title: A woman and a slave are liable; they just cannot pay yet
steps.stepSummary: רבינא's side answers that a woman and a slave really are subject to liability. They only lack money right now, as a משנה shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can say: a woman and a slave are subject to liability. It is only that right now they have nothing to pay with. As we learned in a משנה: if the woman gets divorced, or the slave is freed, they must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבינא against the challenge in step 16. A woman and a slave are not like a courtyard, because they really are liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that a woman and a slave are 'not subject to liability,' just like a courtyard. The answer separates two things: being liable and being able to pay. They are liable, but they have no money of their own right now, and the משנה proves they pay once they are divorced or freed.

keyTerms.meaning: people who can be held liable
to pay
she became divorced
he was freed (a slave)
as we learned in a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'not liable' with 'cannot pay right now.' A woman and a slave owe the money; collecting it simply has to wait.

phrases.english: You can say: a woman and a slave
are subject to liability,
it is just that right now they have nothing to pay with.
phrases.notes: A married woman's property and a slave's property belong to the husband and the master, so they have nothing of their own to pay from.

phrases.english: As we learned in a משנה:
If the woman became divorced, or the slave was freed,
they are obligated to pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרַתְּ אִשָּׁה וְעֶבֶד בְּנֵי חִיּוּבָא נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 against רבינא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: liable but unable to pay is different from not liable at all.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A woman and a slave are not subject to liability, so by רבינא's rule the person who sent them should be liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: A woman and a slave are liable and only lack money for now. So אין שליח לדבר עבירה still applies to them, unlike a courtyard.

steps.title: רב סמא: the rule applies only when the agent has a free choice
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא gives a different answer. אין שליח לדבר עבירה applies only to an agent who can choose to act or not. A courtyard has no choice, so its owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סמא said: when do we say אין שליח לדבר עבירה? When the agent could do it if he wants and not do it if he wants. But a courtyard, where things are placed without its consent, makes its sender liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב סמא offers a second answer to the question from the ברייתא about the thief's courtyard (step 14).
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's test was whether the agent can be held liable. רב סמא's test is whether the agent has free choice. A person who chooses to sin carries the blame himself, but a courtyard simply receives whatever is put in it. So the owner is responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: the אמורא who gives the second answer
if he wants, he does it
against its will, without its consent
one places (something)
the one who sent him

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives us a second way to understand why אין שליח לדבר עבירה exists: the agent's own free choice breaks the connection to the sender.

phrases.english: רב סמא said:

phrases.aramaic: הֵיכָא אָמְרִינַן אֵין שָׁלִיחַ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה –
phrases.english: Where do we say there is no agency for a sin?
Where, if he wants, he does it
and if he wants, he does not do it,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל חָצֵר דִּבְעַל כֻּרְחֵיהּ מוֹתֵיב בַּהּ,
phrases.english: but a courtyard, where one places things in it without its consent,
its sender is liable.
phrases.notes: Here 'its sender' means the courtyard's owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב סַמָּא אָמַר הֵיכָא אָמְרִינַן אֵין שָׁלִיחַ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from רבינא's to the same question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the scope of a rule: it depends on the agent's free will.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If a חצר is a שליח, then אין שליח לדבר עבירה should exempt the thief whose courtyard took the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule applies only to an agent with free choice. A courtyard has none, so the owner is liable.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two answers?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבינא and רב סמא would give different results.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks whether the two answers ever lead to a different ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both answers explain the courtyard case equally well. So the גמרא looks for a case where the two tests (can the agent be held liable, and does the agent have a free choice) split apart.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the answers of steps 15 and 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where רבינא's answer and רב סמא's answer would lead to different rulings.

steps.title: Two cases: a כהן and a divorcee, and a woman cutting a boy's hair
steps.stepSummary: The difference shows up when the agent is not personally forbidden to do the act. One case is a כהן who sends an ישראל to marry a גרושה for him. The other is a man who tells a woman to round a boy's פאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them in the case of a כהן who told an ישראל: 'Go and marry a divorced woman for me.' Or in the case of a man who told a woman: 'Round the corners of a boy's head for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two cases where the agent is not personally bound by the prohibition. These are the cases where the two answers split.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ישראל may marry a גרושה; only a כהן may not. The ban on rounding the פאות applies to men, not to women. In both cases the agent has free choice, but the agent is not subject to liability for this act.

keyTerms.meaning: a priest
a divorced woman, whom a כהן may not marry
betroth, marry
round off (the corners of the head)
a minor, a young boy

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
in a כהן who said to an ישראל:
'Go out and betroth a divorced woman for me,'

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי אִישׁ דְּאָמַר לַהּ לְאִשָּׁה:
phrases.english: or a man who said to a woman:
'Round the corners of the head of a boy for me.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ כֹּהֵן דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two answers differ when the agent has free choice but is not personally forbidden: an ישראל marrying a גרושה for a כהן, or a woman rounding a boy's head for a man.

steps.title: How each view rules in these two cases
steps.stepSummary: By רב סמא, the agent had free choice, so the sender is not liable. By רבינא, the agent is not subject to liability, so the sender is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: By the version that says the sender is not liable whenever the agent could choose to act or not: here too the agents could choose, so their sender is not liable. By the version that says the sender is liable whenever the agent is not subject to liability: here too the agents are not subject to liability, so their sender is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out how each answer rules in the two cases from step 20.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב סמא looks only at free choice, and the ישראל and the woman both had a choice, so the sender is exempt. רבינא looks at whether the agent is liable. The ישראל and the woman are not, so the agency works and the sender carries the sin.

keyTerms.meaning: version, formulation of an answer
the one who sent them
someone who can be held liable

steps.whatToRemember: רבינא: אין שליח לדבר עבירה applies only if the agent is liable himself. רב סמא: it applies only if the agent has a free choice. When the agent has a choice but is not liable (the כהן and the גרושה, the boy's פאות), רבינא makes the sender liable and רב סמא exempts him.

phrases.english: these too, since they are not subject to liability,

steps.triggerLanguage: לְהָךְ לִישָּׁנָא דְּאָמַר כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּאִי בָּעֵי עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the cases of step 20 come out under each view.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב סמא exempts the sender because the agent had free choice. רבינא makes the sender liable because the agent is not subject to liability.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two answers split when the agent has free will but is not bound by the prohibition.

steps.title: Does anyone really deny that a courtyard is like a hand?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how anyone could hold that a חצר is not included as an extension of a person's יד. A ברייתא about גט shows that her roof, courtyard and enclosure all count, from the word ״וְנָתַן״.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is there really anyone who says a courtyard was not included because it counts as her hand? Here is a ברייתא: The verse says 'in her hand.' That would only teach her actual hand. How do we know that her roof, her courtyard and her enclosure also work? The verse says 'and he gives,' which means in any way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view that a חצר works only like an agent (שליחות) and not like a hand (יד). It brings a ברייתא about גט as proof that a courtyard counts as a hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps were built on the view that a חצר works through שליחות. The ברייתא learns from ״וְנָתַן״ that a גט placed in her roof, courtyard or enclosure works just as if it were placed in her hand. That suggests a חצר is an extension of a person's יד, and that seems to clash with the view that it works through שליחות.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard or private property that can acquire things for its owner
Her hand; here, the idea that a courtyard is an extension of her hand
Was included (by a word in the פסוק)
A bill of divorce
An enclosed area, usually behind a house, used for storage
The verse teaches; it introduces the source in the פסוק

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two ways a courtyard might work. 'Because of her hand' (יד) means the courtyard is like part of her body. 'Because of agency' (שליחות) means the courtyard is like a messenger acting for her. The question here is which of these is the true reason.

phrases.english: But is there anyone who says
that a courtyard was not included because it counts as her hand?
But it was taught in a baraita:
'Her hand': I would only know her actual hand.
phrases.notes: The words come from the פסוק about divorce, דברים 24:1.

phrases.english: Her roof, her courtyard and her enclosure, from where do we know these?
The verse says 'and he gives,' meaning in any way!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the agency side of the dispute explained in step 12 (אבא כהן ברדלא's view), which steps 13-21 had defended.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation in step 12 that אבא כהן ברדלא holds a חצר works through שליחות and not as her יד
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא learns from ״וְנָתַן״ that a woman's courtyard acquires a גט for her just like her hand. So a חצר is treated like a hand.

steps.title: Everyone agrees about divorce; the dispute is about found items
steps.stepSummary: For גט, everyone agrees that a חצר counts like her יד. The disagreement is only about acquiring a מציאה through one's courtyard. The גמרא begins to explain the first view.
steps.simpleTranslation: When it comes to a bill of divorce, everyone agrees that a courtyard was included because it counts as her hand. Where they disagree is about a found item. One master holds:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the dispute. Everyone accepts the ברייתא about גט; the argument is only about מציאה. The last words, ״מָר סָבַר״, set up the explanation of each side, which continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא proves only that for גט a courtyard counts like a hand, and no one disputes that. For a found item, which has no פסוק like ״וְנָתַן״, there is room to argue whether a courtyard works as a hand or through שליחות. So the ברייתא does not disprove the view that was challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone; all opinions agree
They disagree
A found, ownerless item
One master holds; it opens one side of a dispute

steps.whatToRemember: For גט, a חצר clearly counts like the woman's hand, because of the word ״וְנָתַן״. The question of whether a חצר is יד or שליחות is argued only for מציאה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer keeps the explanation of the מחלוקת in step 12, and its defense in steps 13-21, standing, because the agency view is now limited to the area of מציאה.

phrases.aramaic: לְעִנְיַן גֵּט כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
phrases.english: Regarding a bill of divorce, everyone agrees
that a courtyard was included because it counts as her hand;
where they disagree is about a found item.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעִנְיַן גֵּט כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 by limiting the dispute to מציאה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the dispute: גט versus מציאה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the dispute about whether a חצר is יד or שליחות applies everywhere, including גט, so the ברייתא would disprove one side.
steps.terutzMaskana: For גט, everyone agrees a חצר counts as יד, based on ״וְנָתַן״. The dispute applies only to מציאה.
